title: Quality evaluations only ever run pre-deployment, so a routing or runtime change that manifests only in production has no detector
problem: My eval suite is green and my users are telling me the model got worse, because what broke is a serving-path decision -- which pool answered the request, which accelerator, which runtime flag -- and my evals only ever ran against one configuration in CI.
symptom: Degradation is reported by users and on social media before any internal signal fires. The suspect change is a routine infrastructure or load-balancing edit that no eval covers, so nobody connects the reports to a deploy, and the affected fraction of traffic can grow for weeks while offline benchmarks stay green.
why_now: Eval suites were built as pre-merge gates against one configuration. Production serving now fans one model across several backends, context tiers, routing pools and compiler flags, so the configuration that answers a real user request is frequently a configuration no eval has ever executed against. The gate is in the wrong place, not merely too weak.
existing: Canary deployments sample the new build, but a misrouting defect is a property of the routing decision rather than of the build, so a healthy canary proves nothing about it.
Offline benchmark suites in CI run against a single configuration and are typically too noisy to resolve a single-digit-percent quality regression.
Uptime and latency probes run continuously against production, which is why nobody notices that the quality suite does not.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: Although we run regular evaluations on our systems, we will run them continuously on true production systems
evidence.note: The vendor's own remediation is to move the evaluations onto production, which states the gap plainly: the suite existed and ran, just never where the defect lived.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: capture the degradation users were reporting, in part because Claude often recovers well from isolated mistakes
evidence.note: Direct evidence that a green pre-deployment suite coexisted with real user-visible degradation, which is the failure mode this check looks for.

evidence.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
evidence.quote: More fundamentally, we relied too heavily on noisy evaluations.
evidence.note: Explains why adding more offline evals does not close the gap: the missing thing is a continuous production signal, not a larger benchmark.

build_hypothesis: A production eval probe: take the existing eval cases, run a small stratified sample of them on a schedule against the real serving endpoint, tag every result with the routing and backend identity the response reports, and alert on a per-configuration shift rather than on the pooled mean, so a bad pool is separable from a bad build.

check.manual_question: Do any of this project's quality evaluations execute against the live serving path on a schedule, and can a result be attributed to the specific backend, pool or runtime configuration that answered it?
check.rationale: The signature is a project that clearly owns an eval suite while nothing anywhere in it schedules that suite against production. It can be wrong two ways. A scheduled production probe may live outside the repo entirely, in a monitoring vendor or a separate ops repo, in which case this reports PRESENT for a project that is actually covered -- the manual question is there for that case. And the mitigation pattern only proves that something scheduled mentions production; it cannot prove the probe measures quality rather than uptime, which is why a project matching both signatures escalates to MANUAL rather than passing.

bad.ci/build.yml:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  quality:
    steps:
      - run: python evals/run_evals.py --target http://localhost:8000
